name: The Warburg Effect
statement: Most cancer cells preferentially generate energy via glycolysis and lactate production even when sufficient oxygen is available for oxidative phosphorylation.
statementAccent: preferentially generate energy via glycolysis and lactate production even when sufficient oxygen is available
meaning: Normal differentiated cells rely mainly on efficient mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation and only turn to glycolysis when oxygen is scarce. Cancer cells instead ramp up glycolysis and secrete lactate as a matter of course, even in oxygen-rich conditions — a phenomenon called aerobic glycolysis.
mechanism: Cancer cells rapidly take up glucose and convert most of it to lactate rather than fully oxidising it, a shift driven by oncogene activation (MYC, RAS), loss of tumour suppressors, and signalling through pathways such as HIF-1α and PI3K/AKT that upregulate glycolytic enzymes and glucose transporters. Although less efficient per glucose molecule for ATP, this reprogramming supplies abundant carbon intermediates for nucleotides, lipids, and amino acids needed for rapid proliferation.

examples.text: Because malignant tissue consumes far more glucose than normal tissue, clinicians inject the radioactive glucose analogue FDG and use PET scanning to detect tumours by their elevated uptake — a direct application of the Warburg effect, with over 90% of human cancers showing increased FDG uptake.
Warburg’s own early-1920s experiments using manometry showed malignant tumour tissue consumed glucose and produced lactate at high rates even when oxygen was plentiful, in contrast to normal tissue.
Activation of oncogenes such as MYC and RAS directly upregulates glycolytic enzymes and glucose transporters in tumour cells, mechanistically linking genetic transformation to the Warburg phenotype.

whyItMatters: The effect underlies a major clinical imaging technology (FDG-PET) used routinely to detect and stage cancers, and it has driven a large research effort into targeting cancer-specific metabolism therapeutically.
limits: It is now generally understood as a downstream consequence of oncogenic transformation rather than, as Warburg originally proposed, a root cause of cancer from damaged respiration. Not all tumours show it uniformly, and mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in cancer cells is often still functional and used alongside glycolysis.
misreadings: It is commonly and incorrectly used to justify claims that cutting dietary sugar or carbohydrates alone can starve or cure cancer; current evidence does not support this as a viable treatment strategy.
origin: First reported by German biochemist Otto Heinrich Warburg in the early-to-mid 1920s (commonly dated 1923–1924, with fuller publication in 1930); Warburg received the 1931 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his work on respiratory enzymes.

sources.text: Warburg effect (oncology), Wikipedia. — the aerobic-glycolysis definition, Warburg’s 1920s discovery and 1931 Nobel Prize, the FDG-PET link, and the dietary-cure caution.
"The Warburg effect 97 years after its discovery," PMC. — the dating to 1923 and the oncogene-driven mechanisms.
